processing: Lightly oxidised (roughly 15–20%), pan-fired, ball-rolled and dried, usually machine-harvested and largely machine-processed; a light roast is sometimes added to settle the aroma.
harvest_season: Picked five or six times a year at 300–400 m; spring and winter pickings are the best, summer leaf mostly goes to drink shops and bottled tea.
appearance_dry: Medium-tight dark-green balls with a slightly dull surface and a strong floral smell straight from the bag.
appearance_wet: Thin, soft, bright-green leaves, often with a few broken pieces from machine harvesting.
taste_profile: A gardenia-and-jasmine perfume that leaps out of the first steep, over a light, slightly thin body with a quick sweetness; it can turn bitter if pushed.

brewing.notes: Water a touch below the boil and short steeps; it is all about the aroma and does not have the depth for long infusions. Cold-brews beautifully, which is how most of it is drunk in Taiwan.

vintage_note: Sold year-round, often without a season stated, in bulk and in cheap vacuum packs; spring and winter pickings of the current year cost a little more and are worth asking for. It is a fresh tea to drink within a year, never aged, and it also appears as the base of GABA tea, osmanthus oolong and roasted Dong Ding-style tea.
description:
Si Ji Chun, 'spring in all four seasons', is the workhorse cultivar of the Taiwanese lowlands and the tea you have most likely drunk without knowing it: the base 'green' or 'oolong' in most bubble-tea shops is Si Ji Chun from the Songboling plateau in Mingjian Township, Nantou. It is a rolled, lightly oxidised oolong with an almost perfumed floral nose, cheap because the bush is a relentless grower.

The cultivar was not bred by the research station; it was spotted as a chance seedling in a Muzha garden in Taipei in the second half of the last century, propagated because it sprouted early and often, and spread across Mingjian through the 1980s and 1990s. At 300 to 400 metres it can be picked five or six times a year, by machine, and processed largely by machine too: a short wither, light oxidation, pan-firing, ball-rolling and drying, sometimes with a light roast to settle the aroma.

The cup is all about the nose, a gardenia-and-jasmine fragrance that leaps out of the first steep, over a light, slightly thin body with a quick sweetness. It is less deep than Qing Xin and can turn bitter if steeped long or very hot, so use water a touch below the boil, keep the steeps short and do not expect more than four or five. It cold-brews beautifully, which is how most of it is drunk in Taiwan.

It is sold year-round and often without a season stated; spring and winter pickings are the best and cost a little more, and summer leaf goes to the drink shops. Because the bush is so fragrant, Si Ji Chun is frequently sold under grander names, as 'Dong Ding' or even as high-mountain tea; the perfume-like intensity and the lighter body usually give it away. Buy it as what it is and it is excellent value.

It also turns up as the base for GABA tea, honey-black, osmanthus oolong and roasted Dong Ding-style tea, where the aroma holds up well to processing.
sources_note: The Muzha chance-seedling origin is the standard account; the name of the farmer credited with finding it is not given because I am not certain of it.
